title: Mu'adh ibn Jabal
hookLine: sent to Yemen and asked how he would judge: by the book, then the sunnah, then his own reasoning (Abu Dawud)

cards: A man is about to ride south to Yemen, far from Medina, where he will be the one people bring their quarrels to. There will be no running back to ask.
Before he goes, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, stops him with a question, the kind a teacher asks just before the exam. How will you judge, when a case comes to you?
The man's answer is short, and it comes in three steps. Today: Mu'adh ibn Jabal.

teach.b: Abu Dawud records the conversation. How will you judge? By the book of God, Mu'adh says.
And if you don't find it in the book of God?
Then by the sunnah of the Messenger of God. And if you don't find it in the sunnah, or in the book?
Then I will use my own reasoning, Mu'adh says, and I will not fall short.

And the Prophet, the report says, struck him on the chest and praised God for guiding the messenger of His Messenger to what pleases the Messenger of God. The book first. Then the example of the Prophet.
And only then, when both are silent on the case in front of you, your own careful thinking, done honestly and with effort.
Hadith scholars have discussed the strength of this report's chain; some accept it and some question it.
Its shape is clear, though, and some readers take a habit from it even outside a courtroom: not jumping straight to one's own opinion.
Sahih al-Bukhari adds the advice the Prophet gave Mu'adh and Abu Musa when they set out for Yemen: make things easy, and do not make them hard. Give good news, and do not drive people away.
Work together, and do not fall out. A judge with a method, and a gentle way of using it.

how: Students of Islamic law learn the hadith of Mu'adh from Sunan Abu Dawud as a picture of how a judge reasons: the Qur'an, then the sunnah, then careful reasoning (ijtihad).

o: a ruling copied from what earlier judges said
careful reasoning when the texts are silent
a sudden insight given straight to the heart

games.q: Mu'adh ibn Jabal — tap the pairs.
p: advice for Mu'adh and Abu Musa

s: Mu'adh said he would start with his own opinion
he said the book of God first, then the sunnah, and only then his own reasoning.
the Prophet struck Mu'adh's chest and praised God for his answer
the advice to make things easy was given to Mu'adh alone
Bukhari says it was given to Mu'adh and Abu Musa together.

games.q: you are Mu'adh, about to leave for Yemen. the Prophet asks: how will you judge when a case comes to you? what do you answer?
o: by whatever seems fair to me at the time.
by the book, then the sunnah, then my own reasoning.
I will write to you about every case.
games.why: Abu Dawud reports he gave those three steps, and the Prophet struck his chest and praised God.

practice: Bring to mind one judgment you've made recently, or are about to make, and slow it into steps: what do the facts actually say, what would the wisest person you know do, and only then, what do you think?
Notice if the judgment softens or sharpens. If you pray, you can ask for fairness in what you decide.

wordCard.voice: Ijtihad, striving, the careful reasoning Mu'adh ibn Jabal said he'd use when the book and the sunnah were both silent, and would not fall short on. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: 'striving', the effort of careful reasoning; Mu'adh's word is ajtahidu, I will strive.

carryVoice: Your line: book, sunnah, reason. The order matters as much as the answer. Day eight hundred thirty-five, done.

sources.ref: Sunan Abi Dawud 3592 (Mu'adh: the book, the sunnah, then my own reasoning)
Sahih al-Bukhari 3038 (make things easy, not hard; give good news; cooperate)
